mem.t: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

lessons.title: Confession: Taking God's Side
lessons.theme: Confession is not putting ourselves down but standing on God's side

v: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
He who conceals his sins doesn’t prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy.

lessons.still: Quietly ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: “Lord, show me what I need to confess today.” Don't rush to explain, and don't rush to blame yourself; simply draw back the curtains and let the light come in.
teach: If a patient tells the doctor, “There's nothing wrong with me,” even the best doctor cannot help. John puts it bluntly: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.” In the first stage we saw that the self-ruled life is the root problem; this week we learn how to deal with it honestly in our daily prayers.

The word “confess” literally means “to say the same thing.” To confess sin is to say about sin what God says about it — to stand on God's side. It is not a vague “I'm not good,” but a specific “This is sin.” God forgives because he is “faithful” (he keeps his covenant) and “righteous” (Christ has paid sin's price in full) — not because our confession is anguished enough, but because the work of the cross is finished.

The self-ruled life responds to sin in one of two ways: covering it up (shifting blame, rationalising), or punishing itself (as if enough self-reproach could pay for it). Either way, self is handling the sin. Proverbs says, “He who conceals his sins doesn't prosper.” Here is the change of mindset: confession does not lower our standing; it is a child coming back to the Father. The sooner we confess, the sooner we are free.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Confession is humility at its most concrete: laying down the power to defend ourselves, returning to our place as creatures, and letting God be the God who judges and the God who forgives. Pride says, “It's not my fault”; humility says, “I was wrong” — and that is where revival begins.
q: Who is God? — How can a God who is both “faithful” and “righteous” forgive without compromising his justice?
Who am I? — When you face your own sin, do you lean toward covering it up or punishing yourself?
How shall I respond? — What one thing today do you need to name specifically and say, “This is sin”?
lessons.jesus: Jesus had no sin, yet at the Jordan he was baptised alongside sinners (Matthew 3:13–15), standing among them. On the cross he bore our sin, so when we confess, we face not a cold judge but a Saviour who shed his blood for us.
lessons.pray: Faithful and righteous God, I will no longer say I have no sin, and I will no longer defend myself. I confess that … is sin, and that I have sinned against you. Thank you for forgiving me through the precious blood of Jesus and cleansing me from all unrighteousness. Help me to walk in the light every day. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Before bed, spend three minutes reviewing the day and confess one specific thing
Once, replace “I wasn't wrong, it's just that…” with “I was wrong”
lessons.noon: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous.” — Lord, right now I stand in your light.

lessons.title: David's Repentance
lessons.theme: True repentance does not save face; it asks God to create a new heart

v: Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness. According to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions.
Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity. Cleanse me from my sin.
For I know my transgressions. My sin is constantly before me.
Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.

lessons.still: Read Psalm 51:10 slowly, making it your own prayer. Then be still and place your hand over your heart. Don't ask God for a better performance; ask him for a clean heart.
teach: When ink stains a white shirt, you can't just spray perfume to cover the smell; the stain has to be thoroughly washed out. David committed adultery and murder and kept it hidden for a long time, until the prophet Nathan pointed at him and said, “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7). Psalm 51 is his prayer asking God to wash him completely clean.

David uses three words for sin: transgression (crossing the line in rebellion), iniquity (being twisted and bent), and sin (missing the mark). He also asks God for three actions: blot out, wash, cleanse. His appeal rests not on his own merit but on God's “loving kindness” and “the multitude of your tender mercies.” Above all, he asks God to “create” a clean heart — the same word as “created” in Genesis 1:1, something only God can do.

David's greatness was not that he never sinned, but that when confronted he did not defend himself or shift the blame. When Saul was rebuked, he said, “I have sinned; yet please honour me now before the elders of my people” (1 Samuel 15:30) — still concerned about saving face. True repentance is not sorrow over consequences but sorrow over grieving God's heart; not repairing our image, but asking God for a new heart.
lessons.light: 321 Light: David said, “Against you, and you only, have I sinned” (51:4); his focus was on God, not on his reputation. True repentance is turning from the self-ruled life to the self-emptied life — no longer protecting our image, only asking God to create us anew. Change the mindset and the life first, then the lifestyle: first a new heart, then new behaviour.
q: Who is God? — David asked forgiveness from a God of “loving kindness” and “tender mercies.” Is that the God you picture in your heart?
Who am I? — Is your repentance more like Saul's (concerned with face) or David's (concerned with God)?
How shall I respond? — In what area today will you ask God to “create in me a clean heart”?
lessons.jesus: Peter denied the Lord three times and went out and wept bitterly; by the lake, the risen Jesus asked him three times, “Do you love me?” (John 21:15–17). The Lord was not shaming him but restoring him. Before Jesus, true repentance always leads to restoration.
lessons.pray: God, have mercy on me according to your loving kindness; according to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions. I will no longer defend my reputation; I simply confess that I have sinned against you. Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Copy out Psalm 51:10 and put it somewhere you will see it often
When you are corrected, don't make excuses; just say, “Thank you for pointing that out”
Read 2 Samuel 12 and notice how David responds
lessons.noon: “Create in me a clean heart, O God.” — Lord, right now make me clean.

lessons.title: God Forgives Completely
lessons.theme: Because God's forgiveness is so complete, we can live free

v: He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us for our iniquities.
For as the heavens are high above the earth, so great is his loving kindness toward those who fear him.
As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us.
He will again have compassion on us. He will tread our iniquities under foot. You will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.

lessons.still: Imagine handing the Lord a stone with your sins written on it, and watching him throw it into the depths of the sea. The surface grows calm again. Quietly tell yourself, “It is forgiven.” Let those words settle in your heart.
teach: Someone once said that God throws our sins into the depths of the sea and then puts up a sign: “No Fishing.” Many Christians confess their sins yet keep going back to the shore to fish the old ones out and chew on them again. Yesterday we learned how to repent; today we see how complete God's forgiveness is.

Psalm 103 paints forgiveness in three pictures: God has not dealt with us “according to” our sins; his loving kindness is as high as the heavens above the earth; he removes our transgressions as far as the east is from the west — travel north far enough and you start heading south, but travel east and you never reach the west. Micah adds two more pictures: he treads our iniquities “under foot” and casts them “into the depths of the sea.”

Refusing to accept forgiveness can look like humility, but it is actually hidden pride — as if the cross were not enough and needed my self-reproach to finish the job. Here is the change of mindset: my feelings cannot overturn God's declaration. Sometimes we still bear the consequences of sin, but its penalty has already been carried by Christ. Only those who have been forgiven have the strength to forgive others.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Letting God be God includes letting him be the God who forgives — accepting his verdict and no longer retrying the case ourselves. Focus on the precious blood of Jesus, not on your feelings. Gratitude for forgiveness gives the glory to Jesus and becomes the foundation for forgiving others.
q: Who is God? — “As far as the east is from the west” — how do you understand the distance of God's forgiveness?
Who am I? — Is there a sin you have already confessed that you keep “fishing back up”?
How shall I respond? — How will you declare and receive God's forgiveness today?
lessons.jesus: To the woman despised by everyone, who wet his feet with her tears, Jesus said, “Your sins are forgiven,” and then, “Your faith has saved you. Go in peace” (Luke 7:48–50). The Lord's forgiveness not only removes sin; it gives peace.
lessons.pray: Loving Father, thank you for not dealing with me according to my sins. I give you the old sins I keep going back to, trusting that you have thrown them into the depths of the sea. I will no longer use self-reproach in place of the cross. Set me free in your forgiveness, and give me strength to forgive others. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down a sin you have already confessed, write “Forgiven” beside it, then tear it up
When an old sin resurfaces, declare: “As far as the east is from the west.”
Thank the Lord for three freedoms you have gained through being forgiven
lessons.noon: “As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us.” — Lord, right now I live in your forgiveness.

lessons.title: Forgiving as the Lord Forgave Me
lessons.theme: Both the power and the measure of forgiveness come from God's forgiveness

v: Then Peter came and said to him, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?”
Jesus said to him, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.
And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

lessons.still: Quietly let the name of someone who has hurt you come to mind. You don't need to do anything right away; just place them, together with your wound, before the Lord and say, “Lord, you forgave me. Please help me.”
teach: Forgiveness is like defusing a bomb: the bomb is still there and the harm was real, but it can no longer go off in your heart again and again. In the first stage we learned the line from the Lord's Prayer, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” This week we face it more deeply: how do we truly forgive?

Peter thought forgiving seven times was generous. But Jesus said “seventy times seven” — not meaning we count to 490, but that we stop counting. Paul gives the measure of forgiveness: “just as God also in Christ forgave you.” The more clearly we see how great a debt we have been forgiven, the more we are able to forgive others.

Forgiveness does not mean saying the hurt didn't matter, nor restoring trust immediately, nor giving up on justice. Forgiveness means handing the authority to judge back to God and no longer acting as judge ourselves. Forgiveness often takes one decision, followed by many renewed choices. Keep your focus on Jesus, not on the person who hurt you.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Refusing to forgive is sitting on the judgement seat, which is God's place; forgiving is laying down power and returning to our place, letting God be God. Pride stirs up pride, and revenge breeds revenge; humility draws out humility, and forgiveness opens the door for both sides to win. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than being right.
q: Who is God? — How great is the measure with which God forgave you in Christ?
Who am I? — Are you still keeping a ledger in your heart of what others owe you?
How shall I respond? — For whom will you say to God today, “I choose to forgive”?
lessons.jesus: As he was nailed to the cross, Jesus prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). He forgave at the moment of greatest pain. That forgiving life now lives in us, making the impossible possible.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, on the cross you forgave those who crucified you, and you have forgiven me. I bring … before you, and I choose to stop being their judge and to leave justice in your hands. When I cannot do it, let your life within me do the forgiving. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down the person you need to forgive, and beside their name write, “I hand them to God's judgement”
Pray a blessing over that person, however short
Stop retelling the hurtful incident to other people
lessons.noon: “Forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.” — Lord, right now I hand judgement over to you.

lessons.title: The Chains of Unforgiveness
lessons.theme: Unforgiveness tries to lock others up but locks us in first

v: Then his lord called him in and said to him, ‘You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt because you begged me.
Shouldn’t you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?’
His lord was angry, and delivered him to the tormentors until he should pay all that was due to him.
So my heavenly Father will also do to you, if you don’t each forgive your brother from your hearts for his misdeeds.”
looking carefully lest there be any man who falls short of the grace of God, lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you and many be defiled by it,

lessons.still: Clench your fists and feel the tension. Then slowly open them, palms up. Tell the Lord, “I'm letting go. Please set me free.” Be still for a while, and let that release spread from your palms into your heart.
teach: It has been said that unforgiveness is like drinking poison yourself and waiting for the other person to die. In the parable, the servant forgiven ten thousand talents turns around and seizes by the throat a fellow servant who owes him a hundred denarii — and ends up handed over to the tormentors. Jesus uses this extreme contrast to show us that an unforgiving heart is itself a prison.

The master asks, “Shouldn't you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?” The key is “even as I.” When we forget how much grace we have received, we magnify what others owe us. Jesus speaks of forgiving “from your hearts,” not a surface reconciliation. Hebrews warns of a “root of bitterness”: bitterness grows underground, unseen, yet “springing up” it causes trouble and defiles many — one person's bitterness can poison an entire community.

Joseph was sold by his brothers, yet years later he said, “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). He could forgive because he saw God's sovereignty. Here is the change of mindset: from “He ruined my life” to “God works all things together for good.” This week we have learned confession and forgiveness; next week we learn to be filled with the Holy Spirit — only a heart that has been emptied can be filled.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others. Forgiven by God, we can accept ourselves; accepting ourselves, we can forgive others. Unforgiveness is a fortress of the self-ruled life; forgiveness is the release of the self-emptied life. The self-emptied life overcomes Satan — and bitterness is exactly the breach through which the enemy breaks into a community.
q: Who is God? — The master in the parable cancelled a debt of ten thousand talents. Have you experienced grace like that from God?
Who am I? — Is there a “root of bitterness” growing in your heart?
How shall I respond? — What action will you take today to “unclench your fists”?
lessons.jesus: Jesus knew Judas would betray him, yet he washed his feet and ate with him (John 13). Peter denied the Lord, yet the angel gave special instructions: “Go, tell his disciples and Peter” (Mark 16:7). In Jesus' heart there was no root of bitterness, only a wellspring of grace.
lessons.pray: Lord, you cancelled all my debt, yet I often cling to the small debts others owe me. I confess there is bitterness in my heart; please pull it out by the root. I choose to unclench my fists and hand that person and that matter over to you. Set me free, and make my heart a channel through which your grace can flow. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Read Genesis 50:15–21 and learn how Joseph saw God's sovereignty
Do a small act of kindness for someone who has wronged you
Share with a spiritual companion the lesson in forgiveness you are learning
lessons.noon: “Lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you and many be defiled by it” — Lord, right now pull out the bitterness in my heart.
